title: Consistency and Availability Trade-Off Analysis
description: Synthesize CAP, PACELC, and consistency models into a practical framework for making trade-off decisions.

data.text: Every distributed system design forces you to make explicit or implicit trade-offs. CAP tells you what happens during partitions. PACELC tells you what happens during normal operation. Consistency models tell you how to express the guarantee your application actually needs. This lesson combines all three into a decision framework you can apply in interviews and production systems.

data.title: Steps for Analyzing Trade-Offs
items: Identify the correctness requirement: can stale reads corrupt business logic?
Measure the user experience cost of additional latency.
Determine whether the workload is read-heavy or write-heavy.
Assess the failure domain: can the system operate if one region loses connectivity?
Choose the weakest consistency model that still meets correctness.
Document the chosen trade-off and the conditions under which it could change.

data.caption: Flow for choosing a consistency and availability strategy.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Req[Identify Correctness Requirement] --> Stale{Can tolerate stale reads?}
    Stale -->|Yes| ReadHeavy{Read-heavy workload?}
    Stale -->|No| Strong[Use Strong Consistency]
    ReadHeavy -->|Yes| AP[Favor Availability + Eventual Consistency]
    ReadHeavy -->|No| Causal[Use Causal Consistency]
    AP --> Geo{Multi-region deployment?}
    Causal --> Geo
    Geo -->|Yes| PACELC_EL[Accept latency for cross-region sync]
    Geo -->|No| Simple[Single-region: strong consistency is affordable]
    PACELC_EL --> Doc[Document trade-off]
    Simple --> Doc
    Strong --> Doc
    style Strong fill:#D94A4A
    style AP fill:#7ED321
    style Doc fill:#4A90D9

rows: Incorrect balances are unacceptable; latency is secondary.
Stale posts are acceptable; downtime is not.
User must see their own items; conflict is rare.
Propagation delay is expected; consistency is global but slow.

data.title: Interview Framing
data.text: Start by stating the correctness requirement. Interviewers often reward candidates who begin with 'This system cannot tolerate stale reads because...' rather than defaulting to 'We will use a distributed database.'

data.title: Mistakes to Avoid
items: Choosing CP or AP without referencing the actual workload requirements.
Forgetting that PACELC still applies during normal operation.
Assuming eventual consistency means data will be consistent 'soon' without measuring replication lag.
Ignoring conflict resolution until after a failure occurs.
Copying another system's trade-offs without understanding why they made that choice.

items.question: What if my requirements change after launch?
items.answer: Design for replaceability. If you choose CP for payments today, keep the payment interface abstract so you can swap databases if scale or correctness requirements shift.

items.question: Is there a default I can use if I am unsure?
items.answer: When in doubt, start with strong consistency and relax it only when latency or availability measurements prove the stronger guarantee is the bottleneck.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CAP, PACELC, and consistency models are lenses, not checklists.
Start from correctness requirements, then optimize for latency and availability.
Measure replication lag, failover time, and conflict rates after deployment.
Document why each trade-off was made so future engineers understand the context.
data.takeaway: The best system designers make trade-offs explicit, justify them with requirements, and validate them with measurements.
